positions/cumulative-case-apologetics/on: Christianity is best defended not by a single proof but by a converging set of considerations — cosmic origin and order, consciousness, morality, religious experience, history and the person of Jesus — which together make it the best explanation of reality.
positions/cumulative-case-apologetics/co: No single argument is decisive, but many together are weighty, like a legal or historical case.
Theism is judged by explanatory power, scope and simplicity.
Religious experience and existential fit count as evidence.
Faith is reasonable trust, not mathematical certainty.
positions/cumulative-case-apologetics/or: Articulated by Basil Mitchell (The Justification of Religious Belief, 1973) and Richard Swinburne (The Existence of God, 1979); drawing on Newman’s “illative sense” (1870) and Butler; popular forms in C. S. Lewis and Timothy Keller.
positions/cumulative-case-apologetics/st: It mirrors how people actually reason about complex questions.
It is modest and resilient: the case does not collapse if one argument fails.
It integrates experience, history and philosophy.
Critics argue that many weak arguments do not add up to a strong one (“leaky buckets”).
Presuppositionalists say it still treats God as a hypothesis.
Its probabilistic conclusions seem to fall short of the certainty of faith.
positions/cumulative-case-apologetics/re: Advocates answer that independent lines of evidence do strengthen one another, as in science and law.
They distinguish the psychological certainty of faith from the probabilistic grounds that make it reasonable.
positions/cumulative-case-apologetics/co: Influential in British and academic apologetics.
Shaped popular “reasons for faith” books in the 21st century.
positions/kierkegaardian-fideism/oneLine: Faith is not the conclusion of rational proof or historical probability but a passionate, personal commitment to God revealed in the paradox of the incarnation; attempts to prove Christianity misunderstand and diminish it.
positions/kierkegaardian-fideism/coreCla: Objective reasoning yields only approximation; faith requires infinite passion.
The incarnation is an “absolute paradox” offensive to reason.
Truth that matters is appropriated inwardly (“truth is subjectivity”).
Apologetics can turn Christianity into a respectable philosophy and so betray it.
positions/kierkegaardian-fideism/origin: Anticipated by Tertullian’s rhetoric (Athens and Jerusalem), Pascal and Luther’s attacks on “whore reason”; given classic form by Søren Kierkegaard (1843-46); echoed in some neo-orthodox and existentialist theology. Vatican I condemned fideism in its strong form.
positions/kierkegaardian-fideism/stronge: It honours the scandal of the cross and the personal, committed character of faith.
It resists reducing God to a philosophical conclusion.
It speaks powerfully to existential questions of meaning and despair.
Catholic teaching (Vatican I) and classical apologists argue it makes faith arbitrary and irrational.
It offers no way to adjudicate between rival faiths.
Scholars dispute whether Kierkegaard was a fideist in the strong sense.
positions/kierkegaardian-fideism/respons: Moderate fideists (Evans) answer that reason has a role in clarifying and defending the space for faith, but cannot produce it.
Kierkegaard’s defenders argue he attacked speculative system-building, not reason as such.
positions/kierkegaardian-fideism/consequ: Remains a counterweight to rationalistic apologetics.
positions/pascalian-apologetics/name: Pascal’s wager and the reasons of the heart
positions/pascalian-apologetics/oneLine: Since reason alone cannot settle whether God exists, and we must live as if one way or the other, it is wise to stake one’s life on God; moreover, God is known by the heart, and Christianity uniquely explains human greatness and misery.
positions/pascalian-apologetics/coreClai: We must wager: neutrality is impossible.
The infinite gain of faith outweighs its finite cost.
The heart knows first principles and God intuitively.
Christianity explains the paradox of humanity — fallen yet made for God.
Habit and practice can open the way to belief.
positions/pascalian-apologetics/origin: Blaise Pascal’s fragmentary Pensées (published 1670), following his conversion experience of 1654 (“God of Abraham … not of the philosophers”).
positions/pascalian-apologetics/proponen: Many modern decision-theoretic defenders (e.g. Jeff Jordan)
positions/pascalian-apologetics/stronges: It meets people in the practical reality that life demands decisions under uncertainty.
It combines intellectual honesty about limits of proof with existential urgency.
Its anthropology (greatness and wretchedness) remains compelling.
The “many gods” objection: the wager does not tell which God to bet on.
Critics argue that believing for gain is inauthentic and that God would not reward it.
Decision theorists dispute the use of infinite utilities.
positions/pascalian-apologetics/response: Defenders note that Pascal intended the wager for those already considering Christianity and as a prompt to seek, not a full apologetic.
They argue that acting on a wager is a step toward real faith, as Pascal counselled.
positions/pascalian-apologetics/conseque: One of the most discussed arguments in philosophy of religion.
positions/continuing-revelation/oneLine: God continues to reveal himself through living prophets, visions or the inner voice of the Spirit, sometimes adding new authoritative scripture or teaching; revelation did not cease with the apostles.
positions/continuing-revelation/coreClai: God has always spoken through prophets and does so still (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17).
The Spirit leads into all truth (John 16:13).
In stronger forms, new scripture or binding revelation is given (Montanist oracles, Latter-day Saint scripture).
In weaker forms, prophecy and guidance continue but are subordinate to Scripture (Pentecostal, charismatic).
positions/continuing-revelation/origin: Claimed by the Montanist “New Prophecy” (c.156); by medieval visionaries and radical reformers; by Quakers (the Inner Light, 1650s); by Joseph Smith and the Latter-day Saints (Book of Mormon 1830; Doctrine and Covenants); by Adventist acceptance of Ellen G. White’s prophetic gift; and, subordinate to Scripture, by Pentecostal and charismatic prophecy.
positions/continuing-revelation/proponen: Prophetic ministries in African Initiated Churches
positions/continuing-revelation/stronges: It takes seriously the biblical promises that prophecy would continue in the last days.
It accounts for widespread experiences of divine guidance.
It keeps the church open to correction and renewal by the living God.
Historic churches argue that public revelation was completed in Christ and the apostolic witness (Hebrews 1:1-2; Jude 3).
New scripture claims (Latter-day Saint) are rejected by Nicene Christians as contradicting the biblical revelation of God.
Cessationists argue prophecy claims lead to manipulation, false predictions and authoritarian leaders.
positions/continuing-revelation/response: Pentecostals and charismatics distinguish ongoing prophecy, tested by Scripture, from canonical revelation.
Latter-day Saints argue that a living prophet is the mark of the restored church and that the Bible itself never claims a closed canon.
positions/continuing-revelation/conseque: Generated new religious movements outside historic Nicene orthodoxy (Latter-day Saints) as well as renewal movements within it.
Central to debates on prophecy in Pentecostalism and the New Apostolic Reformation.
positions/closed-public-revelation/oneLi: God’s public, normative revelation was completed in Jesus Christ and the apostolic witness preserved in Scripture (and, for Catholics and Orthodox, apostolic Tradition); later “private revelations” or prophecies cannot add to it.
positions/closed-public-revelation/coreC: God spoke finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2).
The faith was “once for all delivered” (Jude 3).
Scripture is sufficient for faith and life (Protestant) or, with Tradition, transmits the deposit of faith (Catholic, Orthodox).
Private revelations may help piety but are never binding (Catholic).
positions/closed-public-revelation/origi: Implicit in the patristic rejection of Montanism and the closing of the canon; stated in the Westminster Confession 1.1 (1646, “former ways … now ceased”) and in Vatican II’s Dei Verbum 4 (1965).
positions/closed-public-revelation/stron: It protects the uniqueness and sufficiency of Christ’s revelation.
It provides a stable norm by which claimed prophecies can be tested.
It guards against new movements adding to or overriding the gospel.
Continuationists object that it confuses canonical revelation with the ongoing gift of prophecy promised to the church.
Latter-day Saints argue no biblical text closes the canon (Revelation 22 refers only to that book).
Some argue the doctrine can quench the Spirit and make faith merely textual.
positions/closed-public-revelation/respo: Advocates distinguish public revelation from illumination and guidance, which continue.
Catholics accept approved private revelations (Lourdes, Fatima) while insisting they add nothing to the faith.
positions/closed-public-revelation/conse: Shaped confessional statements on Scripture and the rejection of new prophetic movements.
positions/apologetics-to-islam/name: Christian apologetics toward Islam (from Damascus to Agra)
positions/apologetics-to-islam/oneLine: In the encounter with Islam, Christians have defended the Trinity, incarnation, crucifixion and the integrity of the Bible using shared monotheism, reason and Scripture — ranging from sharp polemic to courteous dialogue.
positions/apologetics-to-islam/coreClaim: The Trinity is not tritheism: God is one with his Word and Spirit, as the Qur’an itself speaks of God’s Word and Spirit.
The Bible has not been corrupted (against the Islamic charge of tahrif).
Rational criteria can discern the true religion among many.
Christians can honour shared beliefs while proclaiming Christ.
positions/apologetics-to-islam/origin: Began with John of Damascus (c.743) under the Umayyads and flowered in Syriac and Arabic: Timothy I’s dialogue with Caliph al-Mahdi (782), Theodore Abu Qurrah and ‘Ammar al-Basri (9th century); continued in Latin by Peter the Venerable, Ramon Llull and Nicholas of Cusa, and in modern missions by Henry Martyn and Karl Pfander.
positions/apologetics-to-islam/proponent: Habib ibn Khidma Abu Ra’ita (Syriac Orthodox)
positions/apologetics-to-islam/strongest: It was developed by Christians living under Islamic rule who knew Islam from the inside.
It used Arabic categories and kalām methods, a pioneering work of contextual theology.
At its best (Timothy I) it modelled respect and clarity together.
Polemical strands (John of Damascus, later medieval and missionary writers) misrepresented Islam and fostered hostility.
Muslim scholars (e.g. Kairanawi, 1854) turned European biblical criticism against claims of the Bible’s integrity.
Some modern Christians argue for dialogue without apologetics, or for “insider movement” approaches that critics consider syncretistic.
positions/apologetics-to-islam/responses: Defenders note that Eastern Christians wrote under real constraints and developed sophisticated, often irenic arguments.
Contemporary scholars of Arabic Christianity (Griffith) highlight its value for current dialogue.
positions/apologetics-to-islam/consequen: Created the first body of Christian theology in Arabic.
Shaped Nostra Aetate (1965) and modern Christian–Muslim dialogue as well as continued evangelical apologetics.
